newsitem.title: UK: Risks mount as Mexican peso powers on - Kleinwort.
newsitem.headline: Risks mount as Mexican peso powers on - Kleinwort.

text.p: Persistent strength of the Mexican peso will spell trouble next year if the authorities do not intervene to counteract it soon, Kleinwort Benson warned on Monday.
The currency, converted from a crawling peg to a free float after December 1994's traumatic devaluation, has appreciated by around 23 percent against the dollar this year.

Trade surpluses, successful forays into the international capital markets and a boost to sentiment from the government's delivery on promises of fiscal and monetary firmness, have all contributed to the peso's strength this year.

But in a note to investors, Kleinwort Benson estimated the peso was overvalued by about 9.0 percent against the dollar on a purchasing power parity basis and said strong action was needed in the next four months.

"If the exchange rate depreciation does not take place this year, it will simply be a case of storing up the problem for a later date," said Neil Dougal, Latin America analyst at Kleinwort Benson Securities.
"The longer the delay, the bigger the required adjustment."
He said using interest rate policy to influence the exchange rate was the only practical tool in the short term, but this was causing sharp fluctuations in real rates.
While active intervention could have an expansionary effect on money supply, there was space for this without exerting undue upward pressure on interest rates.
"The current undershoot on monetary base targets means there is ample scope for non-sterilised intervention," he said.

Mexico's central bank has intervened on the foreign exchanges, buying dollars on the open market last month for the first time since the devaluation. But the $130 million purchase was comparatively small and was aimed at rebuilding reserves rather than weakening the currency.
Analysts would like to see more.
"In our view, there is now a strong case for more explicit and aggressive action," Dougal said.

The announcement by the Mexican authorities at the start of August, that they would modify the policy of a free floating peso by buying limited quantities of dollars from local commercial banks, was a postive first, Dougal said. But more action was needed.

"A clear signal and more aggressive action are required if problems for the peso at the end of this year or in the first half of 1997 are tO be avoided," he said. --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
